query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: During elevated-temperature (700–1000 °C) exposure to oxidizing gases with appreciable O2 partial pressure, rapid formation of multi-component oxide scales depletes Cr- and Ti-rich zones near grain boundaries, embrittling the FCC matrix and leading to microcracking and catastrophic failure. In more reducing conditions, oxide scale growth is suppressed, mitigating local depletion and delaying failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix, exhibiting minimal oxidation or secondary-phase formation.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of gas environment from strongly oxidizing (high O2 partial pressure) to reducing (high H2 partial pressure) while tracking oxide development and mechanical performance.
generation.conditions: Exposure temperatures of 700–1000 °C for 10–50 hours; stepwise changes in O2/H2 partial pressures observed via in-situ XRD, SEM/EDS, and thermogravimetric analysis.
generation.structural_mediator: Oxide-scale formation and spallation at grain boundaries with localized depletion of Cr and Ti from the bulk matrix.
generation.mechanism: Oxidizing atmospheres drive excessive oxide growth, causing microstructure destabilization and cracks at depleted interfaces. Under more reducing conditions, these effects are diminished, preserving alloy ductility and delaying catastrophic fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the inert baseline, specimens in highly oxidizing conditions show increased oxide-layer thickness, grain-boundary cracking, and reduced fracture toughness; those in reducing atmospheres exhibit thinner or minimal surface films and retain higher ductility.
generation.baseline: Inert or near-inert environment exposures that do not promote significant oxide scale formation or extensive element depletion; baseline samples exhibit minimal weight gain and maintain mechanical integrity.
generation.boundary: Valid within 700–1000 °C in O2/H2 environments; beyond these temperatures or at extreme partial pressures, alternative mechanisms (e.g., internal nitridation) could dominate.
generation.uncertainty: Whether under highly reducing conditions secondary phases (e.g., nitrides) might also form and contribute to embrittlement remains unclear without additional data.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose replicate samples to incremental changes in O2/H2 partial pressures at 700–1000 °C, monitor weight change by TGA, analyze oxide-layer thickness and composition via in-situ XRD/SEM, and measure tensile properties to compare fracture modes and ductility.
measurements: Thickness and composition of oxide scales (SEM/EDS, XRD)
Stress–strain behavior, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility
Fractography to identify crack initiation sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If specimens show indistinguishable oxide scales and failure modes irrespective of changes in O2/H2 partial pressure, or if mechanical properties do not degrade in tandem with oxide-layer formation, the hypothesis is disproven.

cited_evidence.text: In alloys for high-temperature applications, at least one protective oxide among BeO, Cr2O3, Al2O3, and SiO2 are desirable to form, and that is why most of the alloys for high-temperature applications add these elements to form an oxide barrier for better oxidation resistance []. Previous studies have indicated that Cr2O3 is the sole stable phase in the Cr-O system, known for its compact structure and superior oxidation resistance []. However, it is noteworthy that Cr2O3 was not detected in the in situ XRD analysis conducted for this study. It can be reasonably inferred that non-existence of a Cr2O3 layer caused further outward diffusion of Mn, leading to the formation of Mn3O4, as can be seen from the XRD scan at a temperature of 950 °C.

Similarly, ThermoCalc predicts spinel oxide formation at normal atmospheric pressure and 1100 °C temperature. Meanwhile, during HTXRD in air, corundum oxides formed initially at 550 °C, which is different from what ThermoCalc predicted. The formation of corundom (Mn2O3) during the experiment can be explained with the increase in temperature, and the initially formed corundom oxide changed to spinel (Mn3O4) at a higher temperature (950 °C). If considering oxides that form at a higher temperature such as 950, 1000, and 1050 °C, the ThermoCalc-predicted spinel oxide type is the same as the experimentally found spinel oxide. However, ThermoCalc predicts Co as a second major element in the spinel oxide that can form, but during the experiment, spinel oxides contain only Mn, Cr, and Fe (i.e., Mn3O4, MnCr2O4, and Fe3Mn3O8). ThermoCalc’s predicted oxide structure and chemical composition at a high temperature and in ambient air are closer to the experimentally found results than those in the vacuum. occupying_moves.lever: gas environment (oxidizing vs. reducing, partial pressures of O₂/H₂)
occupying_moves.technique: thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), in-situ high-temperature XRD, and SEM/EDS
occupying_moves.conditions: 700–1000 °C with systematically varied oxygen or hydrogen partial pressures

chosen.lever: gas environment partial pressure (oxidizing vs. reducing)
chosen.conditions: 700–1000 °C, stepwise changes in O₂/H₂ partial pressure over controlled durations
chosen.why: By systematically varying the oxidizing or reducing nature of the gas environment, one can isolate its role in promoting oxide scale formation, internal nitridation, or other phase transformations that can compromise mechanical integrity. Relative to the as-built condition, stronger oxidizing atmospheres are predicted to lead to accelerated oxide scale growth and localized cracking (potentially causing catastrophic failure), whereas more reducing conditions may suppress oxidation but could drive alternative pathways (such as nitridation). Prior studies of similar high-entropy alloys suggest environment-induced phase changes can significantly affect mechanical performance. This hypothesis is falsified if changes in gas composition do not induce measurable differences in oxide or nitride layer formation, or if mechanical failure modes remain unaffected by variations in the environment.
